title: The Evidence
teaser: A senior analyst resigned overnight. The board signs off in 15 minutes.

intro.heading: Case 01: The Evidence
lines: Last night Sam Okafor, the senior analyst behind the Digital First recommendation, resigned. Sam had asked to delay sign-off to re-examine the evidence.
The programme sponsor refused: “We are not reopening the evidence base the night before the board.”
Rather than present a case Sam couldn’t stand behind, Sam left.
This morning there is one email in the team inbox: “I found five problems. I wasn’t allowed to raise them — so I’ve locked them in the attached file. The passphrase is what the evidence is hiding.”

blocks.p: I am told there was a survey. Nobody I know received it.
Nineteen years I have been with you. You write to me about everything else — statements, renewals, changes to my terms. Yet when you decided to ask, no letter came.
If the decision is already made, say so. If it is not, I would like to be asked.

smear.text: Something is smeared across this one too.

blocks.p: Thank you for your feedback. Our consultation methodology was reviewed by an independent research consultancy and found to be robust.
The survey was issued by email to all our customers. The response rate of 11.5% is within industry norms.
blocks.highlight: issued by email to all our customers

blocks.p: Responses were weighted for age, gender, geography and service usage. The questionnaire was available in six languages, including Polish, and telephone completion was offered on request.
We are satisfied the consultation reflects our customer base. No further action is proposed.

memo.title: Unsent — draft
memo.meta: From: S. Okafor · To: the team · Never sent
paragraphs: I won’t be in the room, so this is the last useful thing I can do.

The survey is good work about the wrong frame. 4,812 people answered honestly. The invitation went out by email, to the 42,000 registered users with an email address on file — so 9,214 customers were outside it before the first question. The confidence interval is real. It is an interval around the wrong population.

The pilot’s 81% is also real. The pilot was recruited from people who answered that survey and then opted in, so it is a true statement about a population weighted heavily towards the simplest cases. Put our actual mix of case complexity through the same per-group scores and the figure lands at 73 — under the service it was going to replace. Age doesn’t do this. We already weighted for age. Complexity was never on the list.
The impact assessment makes five claims. Two of them are assumptions in a suit. One leads to another assumption. One leads to a brochure.
And the 3% we keep calling minor is 7,200 people a year, taking six times as long, usually because more than one thing is going wrong at once.
One customer wrote to us about this. One. Most people who are left out never write in.

tally.heading: Sam found five problems.

items.name: The sampling frame
items.found: The invitation went out by email. 9,214 registered customers were never asked.
items.missed: The invitation went out by email only. 9,214 of 51,214 registered customers had no usable email address, so they were outside the survey before the first question.

items.name: The aggregation
items.found: 81% was true of the pilot’s mix of people and misleading about the service’s.
items.missed: Reweighted to the service’s case-complexity mix, the pilot scores 73% — below the 76% of the service it was going to replace.

items.name: The unsupported assumptions
items.found: Two claims in the impact assessment rested on nothing.
items.missed: Two claims — removes travel, automated translation — traced back to another assumption and a vendor brochure.

items.name: The 3%
items.found: 7,200 people a year, six times the handling time, higher cost of failure.
items.missed: The 3% is 7,200 people a year, taking six times as long, with more to lose when it fails. Rare is not the same as unimportant.

items.name: What happened to Priya
items.found: Her point was rephrased into a question she hadn’t asked, then parked.
items.missed: The one you missed. She raised it in the workshop and the minutes recorded it as “noted and addressed”. Her actual sentence:
items.missedQuote: My concern is the people who have never used the digital service — not the ones using it more.

tally.closingLine: The sponsor parked Sam. The workshop parked Priya. The first voice parked was Mrs Wiśniewska’s letter.

chain.title: How it happened
chain.caption: Nobody falsified anything. One distribution decision did all of this.

reveal.heading: What you just did has a name.
reveal.body: What you just did has a name. You checked who the evidence represented, whose challenge was heard, what the averages hid, which claims were assumptions, and whether a small group still mattered. That is equity, diversity and inclusion — not as a lens applied after the analysis, but as part of doing rigorous analysis at all. Most training asks people to spot the obvious. You just did the hard version.
reveal.coda: The gap didn’t run along any protected characteristic. It ran along a contact-preference field — the mundane operational variables are where exclusion usually rides, because they correlate with everything the survey thought it had covered.

blindSpot.title: The Blind Spot Check
blindSpot.subtitle: Five questions for the next set of evidence that lands on your desk.

sectors.title: Where does this live in your world?
sectors.instruction: Pick the closest. Five minutes of conversation, then take the memo.

options.label: Engineering
prompts: When did we last ship something tested only on users who could already use the old thing?
Whose failure cases never reach us because they gave up before anything got logged?
Which of our defaults quietly assume a device, a connection, or a level of confidence?

options.label: Finance
prompts: Which of our headline savings depend on the simplest cases behaving like everyone else?
What does our business case count as a cost, and whose time is invisible in it?
When a number improves, do we check whether the population behind it changed?

options.label: Frontline
prompts: Who has stopped coming to us, and would we notice if they had?
Which problems do we solve so routinely that they never get recorded as problems?
When we say a change went well, whose experience are we describing?

options.label: Operations
prompts: Which parts of our process only work if nothing else in someone’s life goes wrong?
What do we treat as an edge case that is somebody’s ordinary week?
Where does an exception take six times as long, and who ends up in that queue?

options.label: Other
prompts: What was the last decision where the evidence described a narrower group than the decision affected?
Whose challenge in a meeting got written up as agreement?
Which of our confident numbers would move if we asked who was not counted?
